transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I came in because I keep having these nagging thoughts that I forgot something important. Like maybe I left my aunt’s medicine out wrong, or didn’t set up something in my classroom safely. Even when I’m pretty sure I did it right, the doubt just keeps coming back.
When that doubt comes up, do you find yourself checking or rechecking to make sure everything is okay?

Yes. Before I leave, I’ll check the same things a few times—the pill organizer, the stove, things in my classroom, even my lesson plans. Sometimes I just replay what I did in my head until I feel calm enough to go. I know I’ve already checked, but I still go back, and it can make me late.
Do these thoughts feel intrusive and unwanted, like they pop into your mind even when you don’t want them to?

Yes. They just pop back in even when I’m trying not to think about them. I’ll know I probably handled my aunt’s medicine or my classroom materials correctly, but then I start wondering if I missed something important.
Do you feel that your repeated checking is excessive, even though you still feel driven to do it?

Yeah, I know it’s more than I really need to do. I’ll check the same things a few times, or replay it all in my head, until I feel settled enough to leave. But I still feel like I have to do it, even when it makes me late.
Do these thoughts and checking feel unreasonable or excessive to you?
Yes, I do. I know checking the stove or going over my lesson plans again probably isn’t necessary, but I still feel like I need to do it until I’m calm enough to leave. Sometimes it makes me late.
Did these worries and checking start after a specific stressful event or major change in your life?
I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed one specific event or major change that it started after.
Do these checking habits feel like they fit your personality, or do they feel unlike you and unwanted?

They feel unwanted, honestly. I know I should be able to just leave, but I keep going back over the pill organizer, the stove, or my lesson plans until I feel calm enough. It doesn’t really feel like something I want to do, especially when it makes me late.
Do you spend a lot of time worrying excessively about several other parts of your life besides checking, like money, health, family, or work?
I’m not sure I’d say it’s a lot of different things. It’s mainly the checking that takes up my time and attention.
On a typical day, do these thoughts and checking take more than an hour altogether?

I think it can add up to more than an hour, especially in the mornings. I still get through work and family things, but I arrive at school feeling rushed or behind, and my lesson prep and evening journaling don’t feel as smooth as they used to.
When you check or replay things, do you do it because you feel something bad might happen if you don’t?

Yes. I worry I’ve missed something, and that something could go wrong if I don’t check again. I’ll recheck the pill organizer, stove, or my lesson plans—or replay what I did—until I feel calm enough to leave.
When you check these things, does it feel like you have to do them in a very exact or specific way?

Yeah, I tend to go over the same things a few times before I can leave—like the pill organizer, stove, or my lesson plans. I’ll even silently replay what I did. It’s not really that there’s one exact pattern, but I keep doing it until I feel calm enough to move on, and sometimes that makes me late.
When you resist checking, do you get a strong intrusive fear that something terrible will happen?

Yes. If I try not to check, I get this nagging fear that I forgot something important—like my aunt’s medicine was left out wrong, or I didn’t set up my classroom materials safely. Even when I know I probably did it right, the doubt keeps coming back and it feels hard to just leave it alone.
Have you been this way for as long as you can remember, even before the checking started?
I’m not really sure. I know the checking has been an issue, but I can’t say whether I was always this way before that.
Outside of the checking, have you generally seen yourself as a perfectionistic person who likes things done in a very exact, orderly way?
I’m not sure I’d describe myself that way in general. I mean, I like things to be done properly, but I haven’t really noticed a need for everything to be exact or orderly outside of the checking.
Do you often find yourself worrying a lot about everyday things even when they have nothing to do with checking?
I’m not sure. I haven’t really noticed myself worrying a lot about everyday things in general, aside from the checking-related stuff.
When you feel driven to check, is it mainly because you fear that something bad will happen if you don’t?

Yes, I think so. I’ll check the pill organizer or the stove, or go over things in my classroom, because I’m worried I missed something. I keep doing it until I feel calm enough to leave, even though it can make me late.
Do you perform repeated checking to relieve the anxiety caused by these thoughts?

Yes. I go back and check the same things—like the stove, my pill organizer, or things in my classroom—until the anxiety settles down enough that I can leave. Sometimes I’ll also replay what I did in my head. It can make me late.
Do you feel driven to check mainly to relieve the anxiety from those unwanted thoughts?

Yes. I keep checking or replaying what I did because I’m anxious I missed something. I’ll go over the pill organizer, stove, or my lesson plans a few times until I feel calm enough to leave, even if it makes me late.
Do these thoughts feel like they come from your own mind, even though they’re unwanted?

Yes. They feel like my own thoughts—they’re just really unwanted and repetitive. I’ll know I probably handled something, like my aunt’s medicine or my classroom materials, but then the doubt comes back anyway.
When you check things, are you mainly trying to prevent a specific bad outcome from happening?

Yes. I’m worried I missed something and that something could go wrong if I don’t check. So I go back over the pill organizer, the stove, or my lesson plans a few times, or replay it in my head, until I feel calm enough to leave.
